lessonTitle: Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium and Carrier Risk, Consanguinity, Penetrance and Expressivity

blocks.text: In some populations about 1 in 2500 newborns has cystic fibrosis, yet roughly 1 in 25 healthy people carries a mutation in the responsible gene. How can a hidden carrier state be a hundred times more common than the disease itself, and why are the children of related parents at higher risk? Population genetics answers both questions with one equation.

blocks.markdown: **Allele frequency.** Every gene in a population has alleles whose proportions are called **allele frequencies**. For a gene with two alleles, a normal allele *A* with frequency $p$ and a disease allele *a* with frequency $q$, we have $p + q = 1$. Genotype frequencies follow if mating is random with respect to the gene. The **Hardy-Weinberg principle** states that in a large, randomly mating population with no selection, mutation, migration or genetic drift acting on the locus, allele and genotype frequencies stay constant from generation to generation, and the genotype frequencies are given by the binomial expansion of $(p+q)^2$.

blocks.caption: Hardy-Weinberg equation: p^2 = frequency of AA (homozygous normal), 2pq = frequency of Aa (carriers), q^2 = frequency of aa (affected, for an autosomal recessive disease).

blocks.title: Assumptions of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
blocks.text: The population is large (no genetic drift), mating is random (no assortative mating or inbreeding), there is no selection for or against the genotypes, no new mutation and no migration (gene flow). The calculations also assume the genotype is observed or diagnosed with equal ease for all individuals. The principle is an approximation that is useful as a baseline for counselling.

blocks.markdown: **Estimating the carrier frequency.** For a rare autosomal recessive disease, only the affected (aa) individuals are recognised, so the incidence is $q^2$. Taking the square root gives $q$; then $p = 1 - q$ and the carrier frequency is $2pq$. When $q$ is small, $p \approx 1$ and the carrier frequency is approximately $2q$. This is why carriers far outnumber affected people: the carrier frequency is proportional to $q$ whereas the incidence is proportional to $q^2$.

blocks.title: From incidence to carrier frequency
blocks.prompt: The incidence of cystic fibrosis in a population is 1 in 2500 live births. Estimate the allele frequency of the disease allele and the carrier frequency.

steps.text: The incidence of the disease is the frequency of aa, which is $q^2$.
Then p = 1 - 0.02 = 0.98 and the carrier frequency is 2pq.

blocks.answer: q = 0.02 and the carrier frequency is about 3.9%, roughly 1 in 25.

blocks.markdown: **X-linked recessive conditions.** Males are hemizygous, so the frequency of affected males equals the allele frequency $q$. Affected females have frequency $q^2$ and carrier females $2pq$. For a rare X-linked recessive disease, females are therefore much less often affected than males: if the male incidence is 1 in 10,000, then $q = 0.0001$, affected females are about 1 in 100 million ($q^2 = 10^{-8}$), and carrier females are about $2q = 1$ in 5000.

rows: q = square root of the incidence
blocks.caption: Hardy-Weinberg frequencies for rare recessive diseases.

blocks.markdown: **Consanguinity.** Two people are **consanguineous** if they share at least one recent common ancestor. Related parents are more likely to carry the *same* rare recessive allele inherited from that ancestor, so their child is more likely to be homozygous. The **inbreeding coefficient $F$** is the probability that the two alleles at a locus in an individual are identical by descent from a common ancestor. For the offspring of **first cousins** $F = 1/16$; for **second cousins** $F = 1/64$; for siblings or parent and child $F = 1/4$. The probability of being affected by a recessive condition becomes approximately $q^2 + Fpq$, compared with $q^2$ in the general population. The relative increase is largest for very rare disease alleles, because $Fpq$ is proportional to $q$ while $q^2$ is proportional to $q^2$. Consanguinity also increases the risk of congenital anomalies and childhood death in general, because everyone carries several recessive alleles.

blocks.title: Effect of first-cousin marriage on risk
blocks.prompt: For the disease in the previous example (q = 0.02), calculate the risk of an affected child to unrelated parents and to first cousins, and the fold increase.

steps.text: Unrelated parents: the risk is q squared.
First cousins, F = 1/16: use q^2 + Fpq.

blocks.answer: The risk rises from 1 in 2500 to about 1 in 615, roughly four-fold.

blocks.title: Why consanguinity matters mostly for rare diseases
blocks.text: The rarer the recessive allele, the greater the relative increase in risk for the child of related parents, because the chance that two unrelated people both carry it is very small, but the chance that two relatives share it from a common ancestor is not.

blocks.markdown: **Reduced penetrance and variable expressivity.** In autosomal dominant conditions, a heterozygote does not always show the disease in the same way. **Penetrance** is the proportion of people with a given genotype who show any phenotype; if less than 100%, the penetrance is **reduced** (incomplete), and an unaffected carrier can transmit the condition to the next generation, seemingly 'skipping' a generation. **Expressivity** is the degree to which the phenotype is expressed *among those who do express it*; **variable expressivity** means that the severity or the features differ between individuals with the same mutation, even within a family. Examples: **BRCA1** mutations have reduced penetrance for breast cancer (not every carrier develops the disease); **neurofibromatosis type 1** has essentially full penetrance by adulthood but markedly variable expressivity (some have only café-au-lait spots and axillary freckling, whereas others have numerous neurofibromas or other complications). Modifier genes, environment, age and chance contribute.

blocks.title: Penetrance in risk calculation
blocks.prompt: An autosomal dominant condition has 70% penetrance. A man is a heterozygote with the disease allele. What is the probability that his child will (a) inherit the allele and (b) express the condition?

steps.text: (a) A heterozygote passes on the allele with probability 1/2.
(b) The probability of expressing the condition equals inheritance times penetrance.

blocks.title: Do not confuse the terms
blocks.text: Penetrance is all-or-none at the level of the individual (does this person show anything?); expressivity describes how severe the features are in those who do show them.

points: Under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1; the carrier frequency of a rare recessive disease is approximately 2 times the square root of the incidence.
Consanguineous parents have a higher risk of recessive disease because of shared alleles identical by descent; the inbreeding coefficient is 1/16 for offspring of first cousins.
Reduced penetrance means some carriers show no phenotype; variable expressivity means that those who are affected differ in severity.

questions.stem: Which of the following would invalidate the use of the Hardy-Weinberg equation to estimate carrier frequency in a community?

options.text: Frequent marriage between close relatives within a small isolated group
A population of several million people
Random mating with respect to the disease gene
A stable disease allele frequency across generations

questions.correctOptionText: Frequent marriage between close relatives within a small isolated group

distractorRationale.a: Correct: inbreeding and small population size violate random mating and large population assumptions.
distractorRationale.b: A large population is one of the assumptions of equilibrium.
distractorRationale.c: Random mating is an assumption, not a violation.
distractorRationale.d: A stable allele frequency is consistent with equilibrium.

questions.explanation: Hardy-Weinberg calculations assume random mating in a large population without selection, mutation or migration. Close-relative marriage in a small group creates excess homozygotes and invalidates the estimate.

questions.stem: A rare X-linked recessive disease has an incidence of 1 in 20,000 males. Which statement about females in the population is correct?

options.text: Affected females are extremely rare, about q squared, whereas carrier females are about 2q
Affected females are as common as affected males
The frequency of affected females equals q

questions.correctOptionText: Affected females are extremely rare, about q squared, whereas carrier females are about 2q

distractorRationale.a: Correct: for X-linked recessive disease q equals the male incidence, with female carriers 2pq and affected females q squared.
distractorRationale.b: Females need two mutant alleles, so are far less often affected.
distractorRationale.c: Females carrying one mutant allele are common compared with affected females.
distractorRationale.d: The frequency of affected males, not females, equals q.

questions.explanation: Males are hemizygous so the incidence in males equals q. Females are affected only if homozygous (q squared, very rare) while heterozygous carriers occur at about 2q.

questions.stem: Two siblings carry the same pathogenic variant in a dominant tumour suppressor gene. One develops multiple tumours in childhood, and the other has only a single mild lesion at 50. Which term best describes this?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: both show the phenotype but with very different severity.
distractorRationale.b: Reduced penetrance describes carriers showing no phenotype at all.
distractorRationale.c: Anticipation refers to earlier onset or increasing severity across generations, as in repeat expansion disorders.

questions.explanation: Both individuals express the phenotype but with differing severity, which is variable expressivity. Reduced penetrance would be a carrier showing no features at all.

questions.stem: Why does consanguinity increase the risk of a rare autosomal recessive disease more, in relative terms, than that of a common one?

options.text: For a rare allele, the chance that two unrelated carriers meet is tiny, but relatives can share the allele inherited from a common ancestor
Rare alleles mutate faster in related individuals
Consanguinity creates new mutations in the gametes
Consanguinity changes the dominance of the allele

questions.correctOptionText: For a rare allele, the chance that two unrelated carriers meet is tiny, but relatives can share the allele inherited from a common ancestor

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the added risk Fpq is proportional to q while the baseline q squared is much smaller for rare alleles.
distractorRationale.b: Mutation rate is not affected by relatedness.
distractorRationale.c: Consanguinity does not cause new mutations.
distractorRationale.d: Dominance is a property of the allele, not of the parents' relationship.

questions.explanation: The baseline risk q squared falls steeply as the allele gets rarer, but the extra risk from shared ancestry (Fpq) falls only in proportion to q. So the relative increase is greatest for the rarest alleles.

questions.stem: A recessive metabolic disorder has an incidence of 1 in 10,000 newborns in a population assumed to be in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. What is the carrier frequency (2pq)? Give your answer as a percentage (%), to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: q squared = 1/10,000 = 0.0001, so q = 0.01 and p = 0.99. The carrier frequency 2pq = 2 x 0.99 x 0.01 = 0.0198, or 1.98% (about 1 in 50). The approximation 2q = 2% gives almost the same value.

questions.stem: For a recessive disease, the disease allele frequency is q = 0.01. Calculate the ratio of the risk of an affected child born to first cousins (F = 1/16, risk = q squared + F x p x q) to the risk in a child of unrelated parents (q squared). Give your answer as a ratio (fold increase).
questions.explanation: Unrelated parents: q squared = 0.0001. First cousins: 0.0001 + (1/16)(0.99)(0.01) = 0.0001 + 0.000619 = 0.000719. The ratio is 0.000719/0.0001, about 7.2, so the risk is more than seven-fold higher.

questions.stem: An autosomal dominant disease has a penetrance of 80%. A woman who is heterozygous for the mutation has a child. What is the probability that the child will develop the disease? Give your answer as a percentage (%).
questions.explanation: The child inherits the mutant allele with probability 1/2. Given the genotype, the disease is expressed with probability 0.80, so the overall risk is 0.5 x 0.80 = 0.40, or 40%.

questions.stem: State the Hardy-Weinberg equation and its assumptions. Explain how you would estimate the carrier frequency of an autosomal recessive disease from its incidence, and why carriers are much more common than affected individuals.
markingGuide: p + q = 1 and p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1; p^2 homozygous normal, 2pq carriers, q^2 affected.
Assumptions: large population, random mating, no selection, no mutation, no migration.
Incidence = q^2, so q = square root of the incidence, p = 1 - q, carrier frequency 2pq (approx. 2q).
Carrier frequency is proportional to q whereas incidence is proportional to q^2, so for small q carriers vastly outnumber affected individuals.
questions.explanation: The incidence of recessive disease measures q squared; taking the square root and applying 2pq gives the carrier frequency. Because q is small, q squared is far smaller than 2q.

questions.stem: Explain why children of first cousins have an increased risk of autosomal recessive disease. Define the inbreeding coefficient, state its value for the offspring of first cousins and give the formula for the risk of an affected child.
markingGuide: Relatives share a recent common ancestor and so may carry the same rare recessive allele.
The inbreeding coefficient F is the probability that two alleles at a locus are identical by descent from a common ancestor; F = 1/16 for children of first cousins.
Risk of affected child about q^2 + Fpq compared with q^2 for unrelated parents.
The relative increase is greatest for rare alleles.
Consanguinity also raises the general risk of congenital anomaly and childhood death because everyone carries some recessive alleles.
questions.explanation: Parents who share ancestors may both carry an allele inherited from the same ancestor, so the chance of homozygosity by descent rises, expressed through F.

questions.stem: Distinguish reduced penetrance from variable expressivity, giving one example of each from a dominantly inherited condition. Explain how reduced penetrance can make a dominant condition appear to skip a generation.
markingGuide: Penetrance: proportion of individuals with the genotype who show any phenotype; reduced penetrance means some carriers are unaffected. Example: BRCA1 mutation and breast cancer (or similar).

Expressivity: degree or severity of the phenotype among those who show it; variable expressivity means different severity. Example: neurofibromatosis type 1 (café-au-lait spots only versus many neurofibromas).
A non-penetrant carrier (unaffected) can transmit the mutant allele to children who are affected, so the pedigree appears to skip a generation.
Possible causes: modifier genes, environment, age, chance.
questions.explanation: Penetrance is whether a phenotype appears at all, expressivity is how strongly it appears. A non-penetrant carrier passes the allele to the next generation, which makes inheritance look like it skipped a generation.
